# Tool-Connected Design Environments {#sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"We shape our tools and thereafter they shape us."*
>
> — John Culkin, *Saturday Review* (1967) [@Culkin1967Schoolman]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** John Culkin, an American media scholar writing to explain
Marshall McLuhan's ideas, observed that tools reshape how people work. The line
is often credited to McLuhan, but it is Culkin's, a small provenance lesson of
its own. An architecture tool also shapes what a method can change and what an
architect can observe. Those limits must be explicit when the method acts
through the tool.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
What must surround real architecture tools so an artificial intelligence
(AI)-assisted method can use them safely, reproducibly, and within declared
limits?
:::

A tool command is not an environment. An architect can launch a simulator,
compiler, formal engine, or physical-design flow and still be unable to say
which candidate ran, which state the tool inherited, what an unfamiliar
warning meant, or whether a retry repeated the same work. AI-assisted methods
make this gap harder to ignore because they can issue requests faster than a
person can inspect the state around every invocation.

Consider a scoped cache study. It compares a rerun 2\ MB L2 baseline with
3\ MB and 4\ MB alternatives, and only `l2.capacity` may change. A quick static
random-access memory (SRAM) evaluation screens each capacity before the
eligible candidates enter a small budget of cycle-level runs. The tools must
return physical estimates, matched
workload results, warnings, failures, and realized cost. The chapter later
names this example `XR-L2-CAP-A`, but its immediate purpose is simpler. It
exposes the environment problem without requiring a particular method or
orchestration strategy.

The request is precise enough to select tools, but it is not executable yet.
Each represented candidate must become the exact configuration each tool
expects. Workload, software, libraries, process assumptions, and tool versions
must travel with it. Long jobs enter queues and may wait for licenses. A tool
may crash, time out, finish with a missing report, or exit successfully after
running the wrong top-level design. Returned files may arrive hours later and
out of order.

The environment handles those mechanics. It establishes that requested work
reached a named tool against a named state and records what the attempt
produced. It does not establish that the resulting number is a valid
measurement or that the candidate is good. This distinction separates a
well-formed run from a supported architecture claim. Interpreting the return
and judging the claim require additional checks beyond the environment.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Distinguish individual tools and simulators from wrappers, harnesses, and
  complete tool-connected design environments.
- Establish pinned hardware, software, workload, tool, resource, and version
  state for reproducible execution.
- Design typed interfaces that preserve requested meaning and return raw
  artifacts, structured fields, warnings, and failures.
- Coordinate asynchronous, dependent, multi-tool, and multi-fidelity work
  within declared time, compute, license, storage, and permission budgets.
- Distinguish execution failures from design-limit returns while retaining
  identity, artifacts, cost, and lineage for replay and reproduction.

:::

## What Makes a Tool-Connected Environment?

Giving a method permission to run a shell command does not create an
architecture environment. A shell can launch the declared simulator, but it
does not prove that the `3MB` configuration reached that simulator, that the
declared workload trace was used, that the cache and power models match the
study, or that the expected output files exist. A zero exit status reports a
process outcome. It does not identify what the process evaluated.

Five terms divide the work:

- A *tool* transforms an artifact or analyzes a stated property under declared
  inputs and conditions. Compilers, SRAM models, simulators, formal engines,
  synthesis tools, and place-and-route flows are tools.
- A *simulator* is one kind of tool. It executes a model of hardware and
  software behavior and returns only the behavior that model exposes. It is not
  the complete environment.
- A *wrapper* surrounds one tool. It validates a request, translates the
  request into tool-specific inputs, invokes the tool, and parses the returned
  files.
- A *harness* coordinates the wrappers and records attempts, state, costs,
  failures, retries, resets, and produced artifacts.
- The *environment* is everything that connects the study to its tools. It
  defines the state a method may observe, the requests it may issue, the tools
  it may reach, and the returns it may receive.

One environment may contain wrappers for an SRAM model, a cycle-level
simulator, a cache model, and a power model. One harness keeps their outputs
tied to the same candidate and conditions.

The distinction is structural rather than cosmetic. A simulator remains a tool
even when it has a Python interface. A wrapper still serves one tool. A harness
can coordinate several wrappers, but it becomes part of an environment only
when the study can inspect relevant state, issue bounded requests, and receive
identifiable returns through it.

A usable environment must handle four jobs. Setup establishes the starting
design, software, workload, tool, and resource state. Interfaces and wrappers
define what may be requested and translate it exactly. The runtime and harness
schedule, isolate, budget, cancel, retry, and record the work. The returned
information includes execution status, artifacts, parsed results, warnings,
cost, and lineage. These jobs remain the same whether a learned method, a
conventional search, or an architect issues the request.

A caller must be able to inspect the candidate, fixed state, supported tool
operations, resources, and prior attempts before submitting work. The
environment then accepts only declared requests and returns execution status,
raw artifacts, parsed fields, unclassified output, cost, and lineage. This
separation keeps request checking, tool execution, parsing, and run recording
inspectable (@fig-environment-tool-interface).

![**A tool interface keeps request checking, execution, parsing, and recording
separate.** The wrapper validates and translates one request, while the harness
records the attempt and preserves each return status.](images/F6-environment-tool-interface){#fig-environment-tool-interface fig-alt="An architecture question, action schema, constraints, and metric definitions enter an environment as a typed request. A wrapper separates invalid requests from tool execution. The tool path can fail, return partial output, or complete; the parser retains raw and structured output, and the harness records every outcome with cost, provenance, and execution status."}

The represented question and state enter the interface as a typed request. The
wrapper either refuses an invalid request or translates it to the declared tool
path. That path can fail, return only part of the expected output, or complete,
and the parser keeps the raw output alongside the fields it recognizes. The
harness places every outcome in the record for that attempt with its identity,
cost, provenance, and status. Later work can then distinguish a request that
never ran from a failed, partial, or complete return.

Building this environment is difficult because architecture tools carry more
state and return more varied artifacts than one blocking call suggests.

## Why Architecture Environments Are Hard

Architecture environments connect tools that were not designed as one
stateless service. They operate on large, versioned artifacts; preserve hidden
state in working directories and databases; use incompatible formats and
units; wait for shared machines and licenses; and produce partial files after
long failures. A single candidate may require software construction,
simulation, register-transfer-level (RTL) models, formal checks, synthesis, and
physical implementation. No
generic software sandbox supplies those architecture meanings automatically.

Architecture and electronic design automation (EDA) tools often expose command
shells or text interfaces rather than stateless APIs. OpenROAD and its OpenSTA
timing engine, for example, provide Tool Command Language (Tcl) interfaces
[@OpenROADDocs]. A wrapper for such a tool must establish or validate
the declared state before each invocation, use the tool's error mechanism to
return an explicit status, and serialize the recognized fields. It must also
retain the raw transcript and any unclassified output. A clean structured
record is useful, but it is not sufficient if an unfamiliar warning was
discarded while the record was built.

Real projects also inherit intellectual property (IP) blocks, software,
constraints, generated files, vendor models, and tool databases. The
environment need not reveal protected
contents beyond the study's authorization, but it must preserve the exact
identity, version, permitted use, and dependent state carried into each
invocation. Otherwise a repeated request can appear identical while running
against a different design or model.

One legacy SRAM macro, for example, may appear as a behavioral model in
simulation, a Liberty timing and power view during synthesis and timing
analysis, and a Library Exchange Format (LEF) physical view during placement
and routing. Updating the
behavioral model while retaining an older Liberty or LEF view lets different
tool stages evaluate different versions of what the study treats as one macro.
The environment must bind compatible views to one identity or refuse the run.

Translation must be exact or refused. If the study asks for `l2.capacity=3MB`,
the wrapper may serialize that value into an SRAM configuration file and a
simulator parameter. It may not silently round the value to the nearest
supported capacity, change associativity to make the configuration legal, or
substitute another simulator because it is idle. Each of those choices changes
the meaning of the request. A syntax-preserving repair may create a new request
artifact or execution attempt while retaining the candidate identity. A repair
that changes architecture meaning creates a new candidate and returns to method
selection.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="One cache request, several exact translations"}
The `3MB` candidate becomes one `SRAM-A` input under the process, voltage, and
temperature condition `PVT-A` and, if the
predeclared routing condition permits, one `SIM-A` configuration linked to
`CACHE-A`, `PM-A`, `XR-TRACE-A`, and `SW-BASE-A`. The wrapper may change file
syntax, paths, and command-line spelling. It may not change cache policy,
associativity, the network-on-chip (NoC), compiler, runtime, workload, or
another architecture field. An exact translation proceeds. Anything else is
refused and recorded.
:::

This narrow rule prevents a common failure. An automated repair can make a
tool call legal by changing the design that was supposed to be evaluated. The
tool then runs cleanly, but the returned result belongs to a different
candidate. Request validation should catch the mismatch before cluster time is
spent. Exact validation first requires an identifiable starting state.

## Setup, State, and Lineage

Every requested run begins from a known state. Source and generated artifacts,
workload inputs, tool and library versions, process design kit (PDK) views,
constraints, environment variables, host resources, and baseline artifacts
must be pinned or marked intentionally variable before the first tool starts.
The run specification fixes the relationship among that state, the represented
request, the tool path, and the returned artifacts. It says how the requested
work will run without changing the architecture comparison.

At this point, the run specification must identify the starting state,
permitted translation, tool path, expected returns, budget, and stopping
conditions. Later sections add the failure, retry, reset, containment, and
retention rules needed for a complete environment. The complete Lighthouse
specification appears in @tbl-environment-contract after those responsibilities
have been developed.

Immutable inputs are the versioned source, workload snapshot, constraints,
libraries, PDK views, tool images, and baseline artifacts from which a run
starts. Mutable work state is the run directory, generated files, tool
database, checkpoint, scheduler state, and other state the requested action may
change. The harness never patches the immutable inputs in place. It creates a
new working state linked to them and records every permitted mutation.

Reset means restoring a declared starting state, not merely calling a function
named `reset`. A clean reset regenerates the working directory and tool state
from pinned inputs. A checkpoint reset starts from an identified intermediate
database whose parent inputs and validity conditions still match. Setup checks
must confirm the expected top level, clocks, constraints, libraries, workload,
tool version, and artifact set before scarce execution begins.

Architecture tools rarely consume the representation in which the study was
formulated. An SRAM model reads an organization and technology configuration.
A cycle-level simulator reads a platform description, workload image, and
microarchitecture and platform parameters. A power model may consume activity
and event counts from another tool. The environment lowers one candidate into
these forms while retaining the parent relationship.

Each transformation record names:

- the parent candidate and request;
- the transformation and tool version;
- input identifiers and content hashes where useful;
- fixed conditions inherited from the study;
- the output artifact and its hash;
- whether the transformation may change architecture meaning; and
- the next authorized consumer.

Serialization that changes only syntax keeps the candidate identity. An edit
that changes architecture meaning creates another candidate. This distinction
matters when a wrapper repairs a malformed file. Adding a missing quote around
`3MB` may preserve meaning. Reducing the cache to `2MB` so the parser accepts
it does not.

Content hashes make exact artifacts distinguishable. They do not prove that
two artifacts are functionally equivalent or represent the same architecture.
Build systems such as Bazel illustrate how declared inputs and
content-sensitive action caches can make transformations more inspectable
[@Bazel]. Nondeterministic or undeclared tool state can still defeat
reproducibility, so the harness records the execution conditions as well as the
hash.

Seeds are only one source of variation. Thread counts, scheduler placement,
parallel reduction order, host libraries, timing of concurrent jobs, and
nondeterministic EDA heuristics can change a return even when source inputs
match. The setup should pin these factors where the tool permits. Where it
cannot, the execution record states what varied and retains enough repeated attempts
to characterize repeatability later. Declared variation can be studied;
unrecorded variation is an unknown dependency.

A larger hardware and software change makes the lineage problem visible
(@fig-artifact-lineage). The same root intent may produce several software
binaries and RTL artifacts. Changing one binary while holding the RTL fixed
creates a new evaluation instance even when the root intent has not changed.

![**Every evaluated artifact needs an identifiable parent.** Software and
hardware artifacts derived from one proposal retain their transformation
history, and a changed input creates a new evaluation
identity.](images/F5-artifact-lineage){#fig-artifact-lineage fig-alt="One Lighthouse intent branches into software variant S2 and hardware variant H3. S2 compiles into binary B2, H3 elaborates into RTL R3, and one evaluation instance binds the selected B2 and R3. Identifiers and hashes distinguish exact artifacts and paths but do not prove functional equivalence or reproducibility."}

In the displayed branch, the Lighthouse intent produces software variant `S2`
and hardware variant `H3`. `S2` compiles into binary `B2`, while `H3`
elaborates into RTL `R3`; the selected pair becomes one evaluation instance.
Replacing either child creates a different pair even when the root intent does
not change. The identifiers and hashes distinguish the exact artifacts and
their transformation path. They do not establish functional equivalence or
reproducibility when relevant state remains undeclared.

Conditions need the same discipline. A return retains the conditions that
apply to its tool and marks nonapplicable fields. `SRAM-A` carries circuit and
technology assumptions under `PVT-A`; an implementation return carries its
corner, mode, libraries, constraints, and flags; and `SIM-A`, `CACHE-A`, and
`PM-A` carry workload, software, warm-up, region, seed, checkpoint, and model
configuration. The environment preserves these fields without judging their
sufficiency. A timing-slack return of $-12\,\mathrm{ps}$ at a slow process corner is not
interchangeable with the same numeric return at a typical corner. The number
travels with the condition that gives it meaning.

The host environment can also change a result. Mytkowicz and colleagues showed
that link order and UNIX environment size can perturb measured performance by
more than many reported optimizations [@Mytkowicz2009WrongData]. An optimizer
with many attempts can exploit such effects. Pinning and recording the binary,
host, environment, and flags prevents an accidental host difference from
masquerading as a candidate difference.

Pinned state becomes useful to another method only when a wrapper exposes the
allowed change and preserves the tool-specific meaning of its return.

## Interfaces and Tool Wrappers

A wrapper turns the known starting state into one narrow tool interface. Its
request schema names every parameter, type, unit, required input, default, and
legal combination. Its return schema names every structured field, unit,
status, warning class, and raw artifact. A capacity field that means bytes must
not accept an unqualified `3`; a timing result must not omit whether its unit
is cycles, nanoseconds, or simulator ticks.

A usable interface distinguishes state from what the caller can observe.
*State* is the relevant condition of the design, software, tools, runtime,
resources, and outstanding work. An *observation* is the authorized portion of
that state, or a returned result, exposed to the caller. An *action* is a
permitted typed request with identity and preconditions. A *transition* records
what changed when an action was accepted, completed, failed, canceled, or
reset. A tool *return* combines the raw and structured output of one attempt
with its execution status. @sec-feedback-verification-trust determines whether
any returned field can support a measurement, update, or stopping decision.

The interface must also state which project state the caller may read and
which fields it may change. A cache-sizing wrapper can expose capacity while
keeping associativity, policy, interconnect, compiler, runtime, and workload
read-only. The wrapper refuses a request outside that action set. It does not
silently project the request to the nearest supported design. Exact translation
preserves the requested architecture meaning; a meaning-changing repair creates
a new candidate.

Standardization should remove accidental interface differences without hiding
tool meaning. Interfaces can use the same fields for request identity, allowed
actions, job status, errors, cost, cancellation, retry, and lineage. This lets
several methods use the same tool path under the same action and budget rules,
and it lets one method move among compatible tool paths without reimplementing
scheduling and failure handling. The shared fields make request and execution
accounting and the structure of retained records comparable across methods.
They do not make measurements, candidate quality, or conclusions comparable. A
wrapper or tool path is replaceable only when its declared capabilities,
properties, conditions, schemas, and semantics are compatible. Each wrapper
must still expose its supported operations, stages, properties, fidelities,
units, assumptions, defaults, and warnings.

Capability and schema discovery make that division inspectable. Each request
and return records the wrapper, request-schema, return-schema, parser, and tool
versions. A caller can inspect supported actions and fields before submitting
work. An unsupported request is refused rather than silently dropping a field,
changing a default, or substituting another fidelity. A retained request is
never reinterpreted under a newer schema. An explicit migration creates a new
request artifact linked to the original.

Errors are part of the interface. Validation errors, tool diagnostics, missing
outputs, parse failures, and unclassified warnings remain distinct and retain
their original text. A typed result makes routine fields easier to consume, but
the wrapper must not discard output that its current schema does not recognize.
@fig-environment-tool-interface shows how request checking, invocation,
parsing, and run recording keep these responsibilities visible.

The environment need not return a scalar reward. A method may later derive an
objective or reward from returned values, but the derived value remains
separate from the raw observations and cannot replace them. A shared interface
therefore standardizes how work is requested and returned while leaving
architecture objectives and interpretation outside the wrapper.

Structured hardware representations can reduce ambiguity when they match the
artifact. Circuit IR Compilers and Tools (CIRCT), built on the Multi-Level
Intermediate Representation (MLIR) infrastructure, provides typed operations
for hardware compilation rather than requiring every change to be a textual
source edit [@CIRCT; @LattnerEtAl2020MLIR]. This is one useful interface
technique, not the definition of an environment. A shared CIRCT operation,
JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schema, or simulator request also does not
make two tools equal in
fidelity. The tool model, setup, and returned property still determine what
each observation contains. Once a request crosses that interface, the runtime
must keep its identity intact while the work waits, runs, fails, or returns.

## Coordinating and Containing Tool Runs

The familiar reinforcement-learning interface calls `step()` and receives an
observation, reward, termination flags, and auxiliary information through a
standard synchronous API [@TowersEtAl2023Gymnasium]. An architecture
environment instead preserves the typed return from the tool and lets the
method derive a reward when one is needed. Neither interface implies that an
architecture step is cheap. A cycle simulation may run for hours.
A physical-design job may wait in a queue, hold a scarce license, produce
intermediate databases, and fail after substantial work. Tool state persists
in working directories, caches, checkpoints, license servers, random seeds,
and generated artifacts.

One request specifies an allowed action for a candidate under declared
conditions. Each authorized try is an attempt. An attempt may be refused before
a scheduler job exists, or it may produce one or more scheduler jobs or
execution segments. Every job and segment retains the attempt identifier. A
planned repeat is an intentional new attempt required by the study, while a
recovery retry is a new attempt authorized because prior execution failed or
returned incompletely. The Recovery section later in the chapter develops the
detailed retry policy.

The harness maintains shared state for pending, running, completed, and
canceled jobs and segments. It attaches each one to its attempt at submission,
before a late result can arrive. The attempt retains the candidate and
conditions. Dependencies are explicit. A compiler build may wait for a source
artifact, RTL simulation may wait for elaboration, and physical implementation
may wait for a mapped netlist. Independent jobs may run concurrently, but
concurrency does not relax their identity or resource limits.

Authorization follows least privilege. A wrapper receives only the executables,
filesystem paths, network destinations, credentials, secrets, licensed
features, and intellectual property needed for its declared action. Generated
scripts, constraints, RTL, and compiler inputs are untrusted until validated
and confined. Each attempt uses an isolated working area, resource limits, and
a process boundary. Cancellation handling must request termination of
descendants, then confirm termination and license release. Until confirmation,
the harness quarantines uncertain outputs, keeps the status unconfirmed, and
preserves enough partial state to explain what happened.

Budgets apply independently to model calls, tool submissions, elapsed time,
CPU and accelerator use, memory, storage, and license occupancy. Admission
checks reserve scarce resources before dispatch. An accepted request may still
be queued, canceled, or fail. A completed run may still be missing an
artifact. None of those process states is a valid architecture result by
itself.

Automated work also shares queues, machines, storage, and licenses with
engineers and production flows. The environment applies the site's admission
policy through in-flight limits, project quotas or priorities, reservations,
and backpressure, which slows or refuses new work when queues or resources are
saturated. It exposes pending work, accepted work, and remaining authorization
so a method does not resubmit merely because a queued job is not yet visible.

The harness therefore needs explicit states rather than one blocking call. A
request is validated and admitted; each authorized attempt is then queued, run,
and brought to a terminal process state. Terminal cause, artifact completeness,
parser status, cancellation status, and retry eligibility are separate fields
rather than additional scheduling states. A process can complete with partial
artifacts, or time out after producing a parseable report. An infrastructure
failure may be retryable, while a canceled job may not be. None of these
fields says what the candidate means until later measurement qualification.

The execution interface keeps the request identifiable across three linked
parts. @lst-environment-interface retains one attempt, validates its
translation, seals the translated artifacts, and then performs setup and
admission without silently changing the request's meaning. The listing shows
the common case in which one attempt produces one scheduler job.

```{.text #lst-environment-interface lst-cap="**Admission preserves request identity:** One attempt retains the request before validated translated artifacts are sealed and any job is submitted."}
attempt, created = create_attempt_once(
    submission_token,
    attempt_id, request_id, candidate_id, condition_id,
    tool_type, tool_stage, fidelity,
    configuration_id, seed,
    retry_parent, reset_parent
)

if not created:
    if immutable request fields differ from the retained attempt:
        refuse reuse of the submission token
    return current_record(attempt.attempt_id)

translation = translate_and_validate(attempt)
if translation is invalid or changes request meaning:
    return attempt_record(
        terminal_cause=INVALID_REQUEST,
        artifact_status=NOT_CREATED,
        parse_status=NOT_RUN
    )

seal_translated_inputs_once(
    attempt.attempt_id,
    translated_artifact_ids=translation.artifact_ids,
    translated_input_hashes=translation.hashes
)

setup_status = check_setup_and_dependencies(attempt)
if setup_status is not PASSED:
    return attempt_record(
        terminal_cause=SETUP_FAILURE,
        artifact_status=NOT_CREATED,
        parse_status=NOT_RUN
    )

submission = admit_reserve_and_submit_once(attempt, submission_token)
if submission.status is REFUSED:
    return attempt_record(
        terminal_cause=ADMISSION_REFUSED,
        artifact_status=NOT_CREATED,
        parse_status=NOT_RUN
    )
```

Once admitted, @lst-environment-execution keeps scheduling, termination, and
resource use attached to that same attempt.

```{.text #lst-environment-execution lst-cap="**Execution preserves operational state:** Queueing, cancellation, timeout, termination, and resource use remain connected to the admitted attempt."}
job_id = submission.job_id
record scheduling_state=current_scheduler_state(job_id)

while job is queued or running:
    record scheduling_state, queue_time, and partial_artifact_ids
    if cancellation is authorized:
        request termination
        record cancellation_status=REQUESTED
        break
    if timeout is reached:
        request termination
        record cancellation_status=TIMEOUT_REQUESTED
        break

wait until scheduler and process report a terminal state
if termination cannot be confirmed:
    return open_attempt_record(
        scheduling_state=UNKNOWN or last_observed_state,
        cancellation_status,
        termination_status=UNCONFIRMED,
        retry_eligibility=NO,
        uncertain_outputs=QUARANTINED
    )
record final scheduler state
record queue_time, run_time, cpu_time, gpu_time,
       peak_memory, storage_written, license_occupancy
```

Recording candidate identity before submission prevents late returns from
attaching to whichever candidate is current when a job finishes. The scheduler
may accept work before the harness records its job identifier. The harness tags
submitted work with the attempt identifier and reconciles its record with the
scheduler before resubmitting. An *idempotency key* is a token that prevents the
same submission from launching work twice; `submission_token` serves that role
here. Reusing it returns or identifies the existing attempt or job. This closes
the duplicate-work window after a harness crash without changing the retry
policy.

Cancellation also remains a request until termination is confirmed. A process
may report cancellation, terminate after producing partial artifacts, or
complete before the cancellation takes effect. The environment retains any
late return under its original attempt. It does not expose that return as a
live observation until the current request revision and budget policy admit
it. A timeout states whether it bounds queue wait, run time, one tool stage, or
an absolute deadline. After a timeout or cancellation, the harness keeps late
writers and outputs out of live state or quarantines them until termination and
job identity are confirmed.

After the process stops, @lst-environment-return records what happened to the
process, expected artifacts, and parser as separate outcomes.

```{.text #lst-environment-return lst-cap="**The return preserves distinct failure sources:** Process outcome, artifact status, parsing, retry eligibility, cost, and lineage do not collapse into one exit code."}
if terminal state is CANCELED or TIMED_OUT:
    terminal_cause = CANCELED or TIMED_OUT
elif setup check fails before or during execution:
    terminal_cause = SETUP_FAILURE
elif process exits:
    record process_outcome, exit_status, run_time, and resource_record
    terminal_cause = COMPLETED or INFRA_FAILURE or TOOL_FAILURE

artifact_status = inspect_expected_artifacts(
    COMPLETE or PARTIAL or MISSING
)

if artifacts can be parsed:
    parse_status = COMPLETE or COMPLETE_WITH_RESIDUAL
    retain typed_fields, unclassified_residual, raw_path, and raw_hash
else:
    parse_status = FAILED or NOT_RUN

return attempt_record(
    scheduling_state, setup_status, process_outcome, terminal_cause,
    cancellation_status, termination_status,
    artifact_status, parse_status, retry_eligibility,
    resource_record, retry_parent, reset_parent, lineage
)
```

The return separates process completion, expected artifacts, and parser status
so later review can locate the failed work.

The harness records resources separately instead of collapsing them into one
cost value. It keeps tool and candidate identity with submission, queue, start,
completion, and elapsed times; central processing unit (CPU) and accelerator
use; peak memory and storage; license occupancy; model and tool calls; retries
and cancellations; and linked setup, diagnosis, review, and repair work. For
scheduler-managed resources, the record distinguishes reserved, consumed, and
billable amounts when available, gives their units, and names the scheduler,
license server, or billing system that supplied each value. Fields that the
environment cannot observe remain explicitly unreported. Human work may attach
to a group of attempts when one setup or diagnosis supports several
invocations.

The decisive distinction is between one unique configuration and the attempts
used to execute it. A retry increases realized cost but does not create another
candidate or another independent observation. The recorded setup and cost must
travel with any returned value that later becomes data. A later study can then
compare time, compute, storage, and license use without treating a cycle
simulation, a physical-design run, and a model call as equivalent samples.

Before choosing a retry, reset, checkpoint, or cached artifact, the harness must
first determine what the attempt returned. Execution cause, artifact
completeness, and parser status distinguish failed work from a complete return
that reports a design limit.

## Failure Returns and Tool-Output Parsing

Tool paths fail in several ways, and one `FAILED` value cannot represent them.
Terminal cause, artifact completeness, parser status, and retry eligibility
remain separate fields. The rows below show common combinations rather than
one exclusive status value. They determine what the harness repairs and what
it hands forward, so they describe execution rather than architecture judgment
(@tbl-failure-taxonomy).

| **Execution outcome** | **How it appears** | **What the harness preserves** | **Runtime response** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Invalid request | An illegal value, missing identity, or meaning-changing translation is found before invocation. | Request, validation rule, and refusal reason. | Repair syntax only when meaning is preserved; otherwise create a new candidate. |
| Setup or dependency failure | The top level, clock, library, constraint, checkpoint, or generated input is missing or stale. | Setup check, diagnostics, partial artifacts, and realized cost. | Restore or regenerate the declared state. The candidate remains unevaluated. |
| Infrastructure failure | A license, host, scheduler, or storage service is unavailable. | Attempt, failure source, partial artifacts, cost, and retry eligibility. | Retry only under the declared policy. The candidate remains unevaluated. |
| Tool failure | The tool crashes, reports an internal error, or exhausts a local resource. | Tool status, diagnostics, partial artifacts, conditions, cost, and retry history. | Retry, reset, resume a valid checkpoint, or stop. Repetition does not prove physical infeasibility. |
| Incomplete return | A stage or expected report is missing, stale, or only partly written. | Completed stages, expected-artifact check, produced files, raw output, and parse status. | Preserve the partial return and repair or rerun before treating it as complete. |
| Parser failure | A retained artifact does not match the declared schema or contains unclassified output. | Parser version, raw artifact, diagnostics, recognized fields, and residual output. | Repair the parser and reparse the retained artifact when safe. |
| Formal solver outcome | The solver returns a proof result, counterexample, bounded result, `unknown`, or a resource limit. | Property, model, assumptions, bound, solver, exact outcome, artifact, and cost. | Hand the scoped outcome forward without turning it into a general correctness verdict. |
| Reported design-limit violation | A completed run reports a timing, power, congestion, design-rule, or functional violation. | Typed violation, units, candidate, conditions, warnings, raw artifact, and cost. | Record a complete return without rejecting or penalizing the candidate. |
| Complete tool return | Expected artifacts exist and parse, including reports that contain violations. | Typed fields, units, conditions, warnings, raw artifacts, cost, and lineage. | Retain the return for measurement qualification without deciding what it establishes. |

: **Execution status determines what ran, not what the architecture means.**
Invalid requests, failed paths, partial returns, parser failures, and complete
returns stay separate so the next repair targets the right problem.
{#tbl-failure-taxonomy tbl-colwidths="[18,25,31,26]"}

The retained record and next execution action depend on the observed execution
condition. Invalid requests, setup failures, and infrastructure failures leave
the candidate unevaluated. Tool, artifact, and parser failures identify
different recovery owners. A formal solver outcome and a reported design-limit
violation are completed returns, not process failures, but neither supplies a
broad design verdict. Every completed result goes forward with its scope
intact.

A clean exit becomes a complete tool return only after the expected-artifact
check and parser succeed. Consider a synthesis script that selects no valid
top-level module and omits the primary clock. The process may still exit zero
and produce empty reports. The harness records a completed process together
with missing artifacts and failed setup checks rather than substituting zeros
for area, power, and timing.

Physical-design stages show why a complete return may still contain a reported
limit violation. Logic synthesis returns a mapped netlist, constraints,
warnings, and early area and timing estimates, but no placed or routed
interconnect. Floorplanning and placement add locations, utilization,
congestion estimates, and a tool database, while clocking, routing, and power
analysis add stage-specific timing, design-rule, congestion, and power results.
The harness records which stage produced each artifact so an early estimate
cannot masquerade as a later report [@AjayiEtAl2019OpenROAD].

Signoff returns remain tied to the tool, libraries, corner, mode, constraints,
warnings, and waivers that produced them. They do not cover properties or
conditions that were never run. Even a complete signoff return supplies neither
architecture interpretation nor authorization to proceed.

Raw logs remain part of the return. A commercial EDA tool or a detailed
simulator may emit thousands of lines. Passing all of that text to a model is
impractical, but discarding everything outside a fixed parser is unsafe. The
wrapper should return structured fields for recognized metrics and failures,
an explicitly marked residual of unclassified warnings and errors, and both a
retrievable artifact identifier and integrity hash for the complete raw log.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The parser recognizes only yesterday's warnings"}
**The trap.** A parser keeps only known warning classes and drops every line it
cannot classify.

**The mechanism.** A new warning about a downgraded timing constraint or
changed clock definition appears after a tool upgrade. The parser produces a
clean structured record because it was never taught the new class.

**The lesson.** Preserve unclassified warning and error lines with the raw log.
A compact return should reduce reading cost without granting the parser
permission to decide that unfamiliar output is irrelevant.
:::

The same rule applies to partial returns. A placement density map produced
before a router crash may help later diagnosis, but it remains a partial
artifact. The environment records what stage produced it and what never ran.
Later measurement qualification determines whether that artifact bears on any
claim.

Once these outcomes are classified, the harness can choose an allowed repair,
retry, reset, checkpoint resume, cache reuse, or refusal without treating a
complete return as failed work.

## Recovery, Reuse, and Isolation

A recovery retry is a new attempt linked to the failed or incomplete attempt,
not a continuation that erases what happened. It differs from a planned repeat,
which the study requests independently of failure. The record states which
inputs were reused, which state was reset, which checkpoint was resumed, and
why another attempt was authorized. A scheduler pause that continues the same
submitted job retains its identity; an authorized restart from a checkpoint or
a clean reset creates a linked attempt. Repeated failure under controlled
conditions may expose a reproducible tool problem, but it does not prove
physical infeasibility.

Recovery follows the failure class. Invalid requests are repaired before a
tool runs; setup and parser defects usually require a clean restart after the
wrapper is fixed; and transient host or license failures may permit a retry.
Retry eligibility depends on that cause. The run specification gives recovery
retries a declared maximum or budget, admission is rechecked, and a clean
restart or checkpoint resume uses only compatible, identified state. If an
upgrade caused the failure, reverting to the last pinned version creates a new
attempt rather than rewriting the existing record.

Safe caching follows the same identity rule. A complete return is reusable
only when its inputs, transformations, tools, libraries, PDK views, flags,
conditions, and relevant state all match the cache key. Partial and failed
outputs may support diagnosis, but they are not served as completed
observations. Unknown dependencies invalidate the entry. Reuse saves execution
cost; it does not establish that the retained return answers the present
architecture question.

The 1996 Ariane 5 inquiry documented what happens when a reused component
carries an operating assumption into a changed system [@LionsAriane1996].

::: {.callout-war-story title="Ariane 5 and the reused alignment module"}
**The claim.** Flight-proven inertial-reference software from Ariane 4 was
reused for Ariane 5.

**The gap.** A 64-bit floating-point horizontal-velocity value was converted to
a 16-bit signed integer under a range assumption that held for Ariane 4.
Ariane 5 exceeded that range. The conversion raised an unhandled exception,
and the duplicated inertial systems shut down.

**The lesson.** A previously successful component can fail when its operating
conditions change. An architecture harness must record the version, range,
configuration, and surrounding state assumed by a wrapper or checkpoint, then
recheck those assumptions for the current request.
:::

The lesson is narrower than the accident. Reuse is safe only when the
conditions that made the prior execution meaningful still hold.

Tool isolation protects both the study and shared infrastructure. Each attempt
needs its own filesystem view, process boundary, resource limits, and timeout.
A malformed RTL candidate can otherwise corrupt a shared worktree, fill a
disk, exhaust host memory, or wedge a license process. The harness traps the
failure, retains partial artifacts, and returns control without treating the
candidate as measured.

Recovery and reuse choices remain in the affected attempt record. The enclosing
execution record joins the run specification and request to every attempt,
artifact, return, and cost, including failed work.

## Returned Records and Reproducibility

An execution record contains one or more attempt records. Each attempt record
describes one authorized try and the scheduler jobs or execution segments
created for it. Raw logs, reports, traces, databases, and counterexamples retain
details that a current parser may miss. Structured fields make status, metrics,
warnings, cost, and identity inspectable without rereading every file. The
execution record keeps both views because neither is sufficient alone.

The enclosing execution record carries the study and request context and the
ordered set of attempt identifiers. Unless noted below, the fields are recorded
for each attempt:

- **Identity, at both levels:** The execution record names the study, run
  specification, request, candidate, workload, software, declared conditions,
  parent artifacts, and attempt identifiers. Each attempt records its own
  identifier and the identifiers of its jobs or execution segments.
- **Setup, per attempt:** Source revision, translated input, configuration,
  libraries, PDK views, modes, corners, constraints, waivers, environment
  variables, reset parent, checkpoint, and behavior-affecting versions of the
  wrapper, harness and parser, tool and model, host or container, and scheduler
  adapter or execution policy.
- **Variation controls, per attempt:** Seeds, thread counts, scheduler and
  parallelism settings, declared nondeterministic behavior, and repetition
  index.
- **Status, per attempt:** Validation, setup, admission, queue and process,
  cancellation and timeout, confirmed or unconfirmed termination,
  expected-artifact, parser, and formal-solver outcomes as applicable, plus
  retry eligibility.
- **Returns, per attempt:** Raw artifacts and logs, hashes, structured values
  with units, warnings, unclassified residual output, and artifact completeness.
- **Cost, at both levels:** Each attempt records model and tool calls, queue and
  run time, compute, memory, storage, license occupancy, retries, and linked
  human work. The execution record aggregates those fields without hiding
  repeated or retried work.
- **Lineage, at both levels:** Each attempt records parent-child
  transformations, retry and reset links, cache decision, and the next
  authorized consumer. The execution record preserves the order and
  relationships among attempts.

Resource use is one part of the execution record, not a substitute for setup
and return fields. Unknown or unobservable values remain explicitly unreported.
A missing seed, library view, or raw report is not repaired by leaving its field
blank.

Terminology varies, so this chapter uses three distinct reproducibility claims.
*Exact replay* submits the same retained request, artifacts, versions, and
recorded state again. The replay record shows that the same retained inputs were
requested. It does not guarantee identical realized execution or output bits.
*Repeatability* asks whether repeated attempts under the declared setup agree
within the variation that the environment records. *Independent reproduction*
rebuilds the run from the stated specification without depending on private
working state, and may use a separate implementation or installation. It is
stronger operational evidence than replay, but the returned agreement still
must be interpreted against the property and conditions under study.

Hashes establish the identity and integrity of exact bytes. They do not prove
that two netlists are equivalent, two configurations express the same
architecture, or two runs support a valid comparison. Those relations require
the relevant transformation record and later check. The same distinction must
survive when one candidate branches through several tools.

## Multi-Tool and Multi-Fidelity Environments

Architecture studies often use several tools because no one tool observes
every relevant property. *Fidelity* describes how well a tool path represents a
named property under stated conditions. It is not one scalar ranking. A path
can offer high fidelity for one property and remain silent about another. A
simulation accelerated by a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) may execute a
target model much faster than RTL simulation without providing
application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) placement or timing signoff. A
circuit model may estimate SRAM area and access time without executing the
workload.

The useful comparison is what each tool consumes and returns
(@tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum).

| **Tool Class** | **Representative Use** | **What It Models or Checks** | **What the Environment Must Preserve** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Analytical or circuit model | Spreadsheet or CACTI-class SRAM estimate [@MuralimanoharEtAl2009CACTI]. | Encoded equations or circuit and technology assumptions, without workload execution. | Model version, organization, technology assumptions, units, and limits. |
| Compiler and software build | Target compiler, lowering passes, assembler, linker, libraries, and runtime image. | Whether the declared source and mapping produce the expected executable artifacts; no hardware timing or physical result. | Source and intermediate representations, target features, flags, mapping, library and compiler versions, diagnostics, and binary identity. |
| Functional instruction-set architecture (ISA) execution | ISA-level functional execution. | Instruction and software behavior under the implemented ISA model, without microarchitectural timing. | Binary, ISA options, input, termination state, and functional output. |
| Cycle-level simulation | gem5-class processor and memory simulation [@BinkertEtAl2011Gem5]. | Modeled pipeline, cache, interconnect, and memory timing under a configuration. | Workload, software, warm-up, region, seed, configuration, event counts, and traces. |
| RTL simulation | Verilator-class simulation [@Veripool2026Verilator]. | Cycle behavior under the supplied RTL and simulator semantics; no routed-delay result unless such timing is explicitly supplied. | RTL identity, testbench, compile flags, reset, waves, assertions, and logs. |
| Formal property or equivalence tool | Property checking or equivalence for a named model and relation. | The stated property or equivalence relation within declared assumptions, abstraction, and bound where applicable; no general correctness result. | Property and model identities, assumptions, abstraction, bound, solver version and outcome, proof or counterexample artifact, and cost. |
| FPGA-accelerated simulation | FireSim-class target simulation [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. | Accelerated execution of a mapped target model. The FPGA implementation is not ASIC signoff. | Target model, FPGA image, host configuration, workload, and returned traces. |
| Implementation flow | Synthesis, OpenROAD-class place and route, and stage-specific analysis checks [@Yosys; @AjayiEtAl2019OpenROAD]. | Properties exposed by the declared stage, libraries, constraints, modes, and corners. | Every intermediate artifact, tool condition, warning, waiver, and stage result. |
| Fabricated silicon or lab hardware | Bench measurement of a device, board, or prototype. | Behavior and physical quantities exposed by the instrumented hardware under measured operating conditions; no coverage beyond the exercised workloads, conditions, and instruments. | Chip or board revision, instruments and calibration, firmware and software, workload, supplies, clocks, temperature, lab environment, procedure, units, and raw samples. |

: **Fidelity is relative to the property being examined.** The environment
retains each tool's model, inputs, conditions, stage, latency, and artifacts
instead of collapsing several returns into one generic score.
{#tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum tbl-colwidths="[19,22,29,30]"}

The consequence is operational. Heterogeneous latency, dependencies, and
property coverage determine which authorized branches a study can afford to
execute. A compiler constructs an executable path but does not return hardware
timing.
Functional ISA execution returns software behavior without microarchitectural
timing. A formal tool reports only the property and model it received, and
FPGA-accelerated simulation does not establish ASIC implementation results. An
implementation flow remains limited to its completed stages, libraries,
constraints, modes, and corners.

Branches count as observations of the same candidate only when their recorded
translations preserve the architecture meaning relevant to each returned
property. The execution record retains transformation, calibration, and
version identities together with branch-specific conditions so another
architect can check that correspondence.

For one prospective `L2-3M-A` environment, `SRAM-A` receives the exact cache
organization and `PVT-A`. The compiler branch binds `SW-BASE-A`, target
features, libraries, flags, and runtime to a hashed binary. The cycle-level
branch binds that binary and candidate to `XR-TRACE-A`, `SIM-A`, `CACHE-A`,
`PM-A`, warm-up, seed, and checkpoint. RTL simulation adds generated RTL, a
testbench, compile flags, and reset. Formal checking adds one named property or
equivalence relation, assumptions, abstraction, bound, and solver. Logic
synthesis adds top-level constraints and libraries; physical implementation
adds floorplan, PDK views, modes, corners, and waivers.

These branches are not interchangeable. Only the SRAM and cycle-level branches
belong to the constructed trace below. The environment preserves every branch's
input, raw and structured return, cost, conditions, and limit without promoting
or rejecting `L2-3M-A`.

Throughput changes how many candidates and conditions a study can afford to
examine. In one published configuration, ZSim ran a detailed Westmere-class
out-of-order model at 20 million simulated instructions per second, about
$200\times$ slower than the modeled core. The same study reported conventional
detailed simulators at roughly 100 to 200 thousand simulated instructions per
second [@ZSim]. FireSim reports a different regime. Individual target nodes in
FPGA-accelerated simulation can run at tens to hundreds of megahertz, while one
1,024-node configuration ran at 3.4\ MHz for 3.2\ GHz targets, a slowdown of
less than $1{,}000\times$ [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim].

Those rates are examples, not constants for a tool class. The modeled system,
host or FPGA allocation, workload, instrumentation, accuracy, and simulation
scale all change the rate. The environment should therefore record the
observed throughput and its conditions, and a method should budget evaluations
from that scoped rate rather than from a generic label such as *cycle-level* or
*FPGA-accelerated simulation*.

Sampling and checkpoint policy are part of that identity. SimPoint selects
representative program regions, while SMARTS supplies a statistical basis for
sampled simulation [@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint; @WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. The
environment records the chosen regions, weights, warm-up, fast-forward policy,
and checkpoint parent. It does not decide whether those choices support the
intended comparison.

ArchGym shows the value of exposing several architecture simulators through a
shared interface under controlled budgets [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym]. Real
project environments need additional state. Jobs wait in queues, hold licenses,
resume checkpoints, and return at different times. A common interface should
make those differences visible rather than hide them behind one `step()` call.

Chipyard provides a concrete multi-tool example. One configuration can drive
Chisel generation and Flexible Intermediate Representation for RTL (FIRRTL)
compiler passes, followed by branch-specific transformations and tools for RTL
simulation, very-large-scale integration (VLSI) implementation, and
FPGA-accelerated simulation [@chipyard]. The common configuration supplies the
shared lineage; the branches produce different artifacts and examine different
properties (@fig-chipyard-framework).

![**A common configuration links distinct authorized tool paths.** Chipyard
retains configuration lineage while branch-specific transformations and tools
produce artifacts for RTL simulation, VLSI implementation, and FPGA-accelerated
simulation.](images/F6b-chipyard-framework){#fig-chipyard-framework fig-alt="A flow diagram of the Chipyard framework. A common configuration feeds Chisel generation and compiler transformations. Branch-specific tools then produce artifacts for RTL simulation, a VLSI implementation flow, and FPGA-accelerated simulation."}

The common configuration and generated hardware description provide a shared
parent, but branch-specific compiler and backend work determines the artifact
that each path consumes and returns. The fan-out therefore implies neither a
fixed execution order nor interchangeable branch results.

A dependency graph identifies which branches can run concurrently and which
must wait for an input. Workflow systems such as Nextflow and Snakemake show how
workflow logic can remain separate from execution on local machines or
computing clusters [@DiTommasoEtAl2017Nextflow;
@KosterEtAl2012Snakemake]. The run specification remains in charge. The
scheduler may plan authorized work, but it may not add a tool, skip a required
branch, or change fidelity without a new request.

Applicable inexpensive prerequisite checks should run before expensive
dependent work. If a declared syntax, interface, functional, or equivalence
check reports that an artifact failed a predeclared prerequisite, the harness
records the return and suppresses only the dependent dispatch before synthesis
or physical implementation. It does not issue an architecture verdict. This is
not one universal tool order. The requested run determines the prerequisites
and affordable branches, and later measurement qualification determines what a
passing or failing check establishes.

## The Lighthouse Environment

For `XR-L2-CAP-A`, the graph stays small. Three independent `SRAM-A` calls
precede the cycle-level branch. The shared 2\ MB baseline and each eligible
alternative use the same `SIM-A`, `CACHE-A`, `PM-A`, workload, software, and
condition identities. An authorized retry creates a retry edge. It does not
create another candidate.

The complete run specification can now collect the responsibilities developed
throughout the chapter in one place (@tbl-environment-contract).

| **Run Field** | **`XR-L2-CAP-A` Run Specification** |
| --- | --- |
| **Setup and identity** | Bind `RUN-SPEC-A` and design revision `XR-COMPUTE-A` to candidates `L2-2M-A`, `L2-3M-A`, and `L2-4M-A`. Give each candidate a complete `SRAM-A` organization record with every required request-schema field, including capacity, geometry, banking, ports, modeled periphery, and exact SRAM model and technology identity. Only `l2.capacity` may vary. Keep cache policy, NoC, memory system, compiler, runtime, software image `SW-BASE-A`, and workload snapshot `XR-TRACE-A` fixed. |
| **Interface and tool path** | Serialize only the three declared `l2.capacity` values into `SRAM-A` under `PVT-A` and eligible `SIM-A` requests with `CACHE-A` and `PM-A`. A wrapper may change syntax and file layout but not architecture meaning. Retain behavior-affecting wrapper, request-schema, return-schema, parser, tool, and model versions, plus flags, host or container identity, seeds, and reset state. |
| **Order, budget, and stop** | Run one SRAM evaluation per capacity. Apply the area and access-time predicate only to a complete, schema-valid SRAM return with declared units. A missing, partial, or schema-invalid return cannot authorize cycle-level dispatch. The predicate is an operational dispatch gate, not measurement validation or candidate rejection. Run the shared 2\ MB baseline and eligible alternatives under matched conditions. Allow three SRAM evaluations and at most four cycle-level attempts, including recovery retries. Stop an attempt when its queue-wait or run-time deadline expires. Stop the study when authorized work completes, no alternative qualifies for dispatch, the cycle-level budget is exhausted, or the absolute deadline expires. |
| **Failure, reset, and containment** | Refuse invalid requests before invocation and keep timeouts, cancellations, infrastructure failures, stale state, missing output, and parser failure distinct. Each retry links to its parent, consumes budget, and regenerates a clean work directory from the fixed state. Grant only declared tools, paths, credentials, network access, and resources; quarantine uncertain output after unconfirmed termination. |
| **Cache reuse** | Reuse a completed return only when request, candidate, conditions, translated inputs, tool and model, wrapper and parser, and retained artifact identities all match. Failed or partial outputs are not completed cache hits. |
| **Returns and retention** | Retain area, access time, cache-local energy and leakage, matched frame records, frame-time inputs, capacity misses, subsystem power, warnings, translated inputs, commands, raw logs, parsed fields, unclassified output, hashes, cost, and parent-child lineage. |
| **Decisions left outside** | The environment does not decide whether a field is a valid measurement, two returns form a valid comparison, a reported limit establishes rejection, or a candidate should advance. |

: **A run specification prevents tool mechanics from rewriting the study.**
The request, translation, state, expected outputs, failure behavior, cost, and
limits are fixed before invocation.
{#tbl-environment-contract tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

The first two rows preserve the complete candidate and fixed state through
exact translation. The order row admits a simulator attempt only after a
complete SRAM return passes schema and dispatch checks. The cache row makes
reuse depend on exact identity rather than a similar-looking request. The final
rows preserve failure behavior, authority, returned artifacts, and the
decisions that remain outside the environment.

This specification must still be written before the first tool call. Filled
afterward, it cannot refuse a bad translation or require a missing output. It
may authorize host selection, license reservation, pause, and resume, but
substituting a tool path, serving stale state, or skipping the baseline requires
a new request.

The run specification states what is intended to execute. The execution record
below states what actually happened across its attempt records. Comparing them
reveals missing outputs, unexpected state, failures, retries, and budget use
without treating an execution record as an architecture verdict.

A constructed trace makes the execution record concrete
(@tbl-lighthouse-execution-record). It is an author-created teaching example,
not live project history or measurements from tools run for this book. It
contains illustrative SRAM and power returns, one stale-state failure, and a
four-attempt cycle-level chronology. The values exercise the record rather than
predict the Lighthouse design, and every field absent from the construction
remains marked unreported.

| **Record item** | **Candidate and state** | **Constructed outcome or return** | **Known cost, lineage, and missing record** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `SRAM-2-A1` | `L2-2M-A` under `PVT-A`. | Area $1.2\,\mathrm{mm}^2$; access time $2.1\,\mathrm{ns}$. | One SRAM call. Serialized input, energy, leakage, raw artifact, parse status, and other cost are unreported. |
| `SRAM-3-A1` | `L2-3M-A` under `PVT-A`. | Area $1.4\,\mathrm{mm}^2$; access time $2.4\,\mathrm{ns}$. | One SRAM call. The same fields remain unreported. |
| `SRAM-4-A1` | `L2-4M-A` under `PVT-A`. | Area $1.7\,\mathrm{mm}^2$; access time $2.8\,\mathrm{ns}$; no simulator request appears. | One SRAM call. Parse status and the exact dispatch event are unreported; this is not a design verdict. |
| `SIM-2-A1` | `L2-2M-A` with the fixed workload and software; clean-state identity unreported. | Baseline frame summary and subsystem dynamic plus leakage power $2.90\,\mathrm{W}$. | Cycle attempt 1 of 4. Matched frame records, artifact identity, parser fields, and other cost are unreported. |
| `SIM-3-A1` | `L2-3M-A` with stale constraint state. | Setup failure; no candidate return. | Cycle attempt 2 of 4. Diagnostics, retry parent, reset action, and partial artifacts are unreported. |
| `SIM-3-A2` | `L2-3M-A`; post-reset attempt with reset-state identity unreported. | A frame, cache, and power return is indicated, but its values and artifact identity are unreported. | Cycle attempt 3 of 4. Retry parent, reset action, cost, and output lineage are unreported. |
| `SIM-3-A3` | `L2-3M-A`; planned repeat with starting-state identity unreported. | A frame, cache, and power return is indicated, but its values and artifact identity are unreported. | Cycle attempt 4 of 4; budget exhausted. Repeat relationship, cost, and output lineage are unreported. |
| `SIM-3-SUMMARY-A` | Derived from parent attempts `SIM-3-A2` and `SIM-3-A3`. | Grouped frame, cache, and power summary with no values or per-attempt attribution. | No tool call. Derivation version, input artifact identities, and processing cost are unreported. |

: **An execution record preserves missing information as carefully as returned
values.** The constructed cache chronology retains candidate state, failure,
successor attempts, the derived summary, and call counts without claiming real
measurements, attempt-level attribution, or completeness.
{#tbl-lighthouse-execution-record tbl-colwidths="[13,22,28,37]"}

The trace supports a narrow chronology and budget account. It contains three
SRAM calls, four cycle-level attempts, one stale-state setup failure, a
post-reset attempt, a planned repeat, and a separate summary derived from the
last two attempts. The 4\ MB row records no simulator request, but the missing
parse status and dispatch event prevent the trace from showing why.

Exact translated inputs and hashes, behavior-affecting versions, starting and
reset-state identities, seeds and job times, parser and raw-artifact identities,
matched frame records, and resource costs remain unreported. The record is
therefore incomplete under @tbl-environment-contract and the execution-record
idea introduced in @sec-architecture-20-ontology. It demonstrates executable
work, returned artifacts, failure, and budget consumption. It cannot establish
that a returned value is a valid measurement, that two returns form a sound
comparison, or that any candidate should advance.

## Open Research Questions

**Preserving architecture meaning across tools.**

- **How can an automated method verify that a tool translation preserves the
architecture change it requested?** Syntax and type checks miss defaults,
rounding, generated collateral, and unsupported combinations. A benchmark
spanning simulators and implementation flows could test whether a proposed
check detects meaning changes without rejecting valid translations.

- **Which interface rules let automated methods use several architecture tools
without making their returns look comparable?** The challenge is to share
request identity, execution status, cost, cancellation, and lineage while
preserving property-specific assumptions and semantics. A useful system must be
tested across heterogeneous tools and method roles, not only wrappers for one
simulator.

**Keeping long-running work valid.**

- **How can an AI-assisted environment determine that a stateful architecture
tool has returned to a valid starting state?** Working directories, databases,
caches, checkpoints, seeds, host libraries, and license state survive different
forms of restart. Observable reset tests must detect hidden contamination across
tools and failure modes before another attempt runs.

- **When can an automated method safely use a result that arrives after its
request, state, or budget has changed?** The system must decide whether to admit
the result as a current observation, retain it only as history, or invalidate
its cache entry. Evaluation across long simulation and physical-design runs
should expose stale-result errors and measure how much valid work is preserved.

**Limiting automated authority.**

- **How can an environment derive and enforce the least authority an agent needs
for a typed architecture action?** Generated scripts, RTL, constraints, and
commands may need selected files, tools, licenses, and machines without needing
unrestricted credentials or network access. A credible system must complete
useful tool flows while containing malformed or hostile generated inputs.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="A reviewable run makes its state and limits visible"}
Start from pinned inputs, grant only the authority the requested tools need,
and retain the raw and structured return from every attempt. A wrapper may
translate syntax, and a harness may schedule, isolate, retry, reset, or resume
work. Neither may silently change the candidate, conditions, tool path, or
requested meaning.
:::

A tool transforms an artifact or analyzes a property, and a simulator is one
kind of tool. A wrapper validates, translates, invokes, and parses one tool. A
harness coordinates attempts, jobs, resources, failures, and records across
wrappers. The complete environment connects represented study state and
permitted actions to those tools and returns.

The run specification pins the request, state, budgets, authority, and expected
returns. The execution record joins that specification to its attempt records,
raw and structured artifacts, and realized cost. Invalid requests, execution
failures, incomplete artifacts, formal outcomes, and reported design-limit
violations remain distinct. Exact replay, repeatability, and independent
reproduction also remain distinct, and hashes establish byte identity rather
than semantic equivalence.

The author-constructed Lighthouse trace records three SRAM calls and four
cycle-level attempts, including a stale-state setup failure, a post-reset
attempt, and a planned repeat. It keeps the summary derived from the final two
attempts as a separate artifact. Missing starting and reset-state identities,
attempt lineage, exact artifacts, and realized cost limit the trace to execution
chronology and budget use. It is not a measurement record or an architecture
recommendation.

Multi-tool and multi-fidelity execution extends the same discipline. Fidelity
remains relative to a property, and branches describe the same candidate only
when their translations preserve the relevant architecture meaning. The
environment can establish what was requested, executed, returned, and spent,
and it can preserve enough identity for replay and reproduction. It cannot
qualify a measurement, validate a comparison, or recommend a candidate.
@sec-feedback-verification-trust takes up that next task by determining how
returned values and artifacts can become useful feedback.
